1:
The chapter opens on a formula the reader of Judges knows too well, and Henry states its theology in a line: had there been no sin there would have needed no Saviour, but sin was suffered to abound that grace might much more abound. Gill glosses the evil as idolatry, the sin Israel was prone to. Henry measures the oppressors and finds them small — five lords with but five cities of note, an inconsiderable people beside Israel, yet as the staff in God's hand they proved oppressive and vexatious; and this trouble lasted longer than any yet, forty years, though probably not always alike violent. Clarke qualifies the servitude. It does not appear that from Shamgar until now the Philistines were in a condition to oppress Israel, or were permitted to; and even now they had not entirely subjected them, since a sort of commerce still went on — they vexed and made inroads without holding them in complete subjection. Ellicott identifies the nation, mentioned so far only in passing and from this point a leading part. They were not Canaanites but foreign conquerors holding a district originally the Avim's; their name means emigrants, their Cretan connection is inferred from the name Cherethites, and whether they were Semitic, Hamitic or Aryan is disputed.

Keil sets the chapter in a wider frame. While Jephthah delivered the tribes east of the Jordan from the Ammonites, the Philistine pressure west of the river continued unbroken forty years, and grew heavier after the disastrous war in the closing years of Eli's high-priesthood, when Israel was defeated and the ark taken. Yet even then, Keil insists, God did not leave himself without witness, among his enemies as much as his people: their triumph at taking the ark turned quickly to mortal terror when Dagon fell from his place before it and lay on the threshold with head and arms broken, and the cities it was carried to were smitten in turn. Ellicott supplies the chronology that locks the period in place. The forty years ended at Ebenezer; the ark had been taken and sent back about twenty years before that battle; Samson's acts therefore fall within those twenty years, so that Eli died about the time Samson came of age.

Henry handles the annunciation with most care. The tribe he thinks significant, Dan meaning a judge, so dying Jacob's word — Dan shall judge his people — probably looked to this man: the tribe would produce a judge though sprung from a handmaid, and its lot lay next the Philistine country, which made a Danite the fittest bridle upon them. The long barrenness he also reads as design. Many eminent men were born of mothers long kept from the blessing of children, that the mercy might be the more acceptable when it came; mercies long waited for often prove signal mercies, and encourage others to keep hoping. The messenger appeared as a man in a prophet's garb, and Henry follows Bishop Patrick in taking him for the Lord himself, the Word who was to be the Messiah, since his name is called Wonderful. The message was not sent for Manoah and his wife, obscure Danites, but for Israel's sake, whose deliverer this child would be — and beyond that for the Messiah's, whose type he was, and whose birth likewise had to be foretold by an angel. Even the opening words are tender rather than reproachful. The angel does not upbraid her with her barrenness but names it because she was perhaps then bemoaning herself as one written childless, God often sending comfort when his people feel their troubles most. And Samson was not merely a son given by providence after long waiting, as many have been, but a child of promise like Isaac, born by force of a promise and faith in it, because he was a figure of the promised seed.
2:
Ellicott notes the birth of Samuel is introduced almost the same way, then fills in the place. Zorah means place of hornets, and Robinson identifies it with Surah, whose conical hill and abundant fountain made it strong and convenient. Gill places it on the border of Judah and Dan; Clarke says flatly it was a town of Judah afterwards given to Dan. On Manoah's standing the sources disagree pleasantly — Josephus makes him a principal man of rank and figure, the Talmudists a plebeian. Ellicott finds meaning in his name, which signifies rest, and wonders whether it expressed Israel's yearning in those troubled days. On family of the Danites both Ellicott and Keil observe that family and tribe are used interchangeably here, and explain it the same way: all the Danites made up a single family, that of Shuham. Ellicott sets the barren wife among her fellows — Sarah, Rebekah, Hannah, Elizabeth — and remarks how many phrases here recur in the first chapter of Luke; from the Talmud he adds that Samson's mother was named Zelelponi, the shadow falls on me.

Who the messenger was, the commentators will not agree. Gill denies he was a mere man, a prophet, or even a created angel, and identifies him as the uncreated Angel of the covenant, the Son and Word of God who often appeared in human form — since his name is Wonderful and he is called Jehovah. Clarke says the same in fewer words: the same who appeared to Moses, to Joshua, to Gideon, and no other than the second person of the Trinity. Ellicott reports a third opinion, Rabbi Levi Ben Gershom's, that the messenger was Phinehas, and dismisses it — nothing can be clearer than that a supernatural being is meant, as in the appearances to Gideon and to Zacharias. But the woman herself did not know it. Angels always appeared in human form, and though awestruck by the majesty of what she saw she took him for no more than a prophet. Josephus, writing to please Gentile readers, turns him into a tall and beautiful youth who excited Manoah's jealousy. Clarke adds a textual note on her report: where the Hebrew has I asked him not whence he was, neither told he me his name, the Vulgate and part of the Greek tradition drop the negative, so that she asked who he was and whence he came, and he would not tell her.

The charge laid on the mother is a share in her son's separation. Ellicott puts it exactly: she is to take on for a time part of the Nazarite vow, abstaining from wine and from strong drink, which means intoxicating liquor not made from grapes; and though the law of clean and unclean bound every Israelite, it is pressed on her particularly, to impress on her and the nation the separated character of her son. Clarke agrees she must live the life of a Nazarite so long as she carried and nursed him, and Gill notes she must drink neither new wine nor old, the reason appearing in the next verse — the child was to be a Nazarite from the womb. Ellicott adds a liturgical detail worth having: when the law of the Nazarite in Numbers is read as the first lesson in the synagogue, this account of Samson, the first Nazarite on record, is read as the second. On the promise both he and Clarke are careful. Samson would only begin the deliverance; Israel was not fully redeemed from Philistine power until David's day, and Samson's own weaknesses made him unfit for the complete work Samuel carried out. Yet Ellicott finds a gain in it: in Jephthah and Samson, Israel learnt what force rests in individual vows to draw out the hidden heroism of the human spirit — in Jephthah an isolated vow, in Samson the devotion of a whole life.
8:
Henry defends Manoah before expounding him. He was not incredulous of his wife's story, knowing her a virtuous woman in whom her husband's heart might safely trust; still less was he, as Josephus unworthily represents him, jealous of her conversation with the stranger. Gill notes a related liberty in the same historian, who makes the woman pray where the text is clear that Manoah did. What Henry finds in the prayer is faith of an unusual order. Manoah takes it for granted the child will be given and speaks without hesitation of the child that shall be born — and so great faith was not found, Henry says, no, not in Zechariah, a priest at the altar to whom the angel himself appeared, as in this honest Danite. Things hidden from the wise and prudent, who value themselves on the niceness of their enquiries, are often revealed unto babes; blessed are they that have not seen and yet have believed. Henry also weighs what Manoah asks for, which is not information about the future but instruction for the present: good men are more solicitous to know their duty than the events that will befall them, for duty is ours and events are God's.

The manner of asking pleases Henry as much as the matter. Manoah does not send servants abroad to find the man of God but seeks him on his knees, and so seeking, finds him; those who have heard from heaven cannot but wish to hear more. The angel comes the second time to the wife, sitting alone in the field, and Henry draws the lesson that solitude is often an opportunity for communion with God, good people having thought themselves never less alone than when alone, if God be with them. She then runs for her husband rather than asking the messenger to come to him: those who would meet with God must attend where he is pleased to manifest himself. Henry finds a domestic moral in what follows. Manoah is not disgusted that the angel did not appear to him this time but willingly goes after his wife; and to atone for the first fatal miscarriage, when Eve pressed Adam to what was evil and he too easily yielded, let yoke-fellows excite one another to good works, and no husband think it a disparagement to follow his wife in what is praiseworthy. Clarke gives a plainer reason for the second visit: it was probably essential to Manoah's peace, who might else have been jealous, and now had proof the thing was of the Lord.

Manoah's question is more precise in Hebrew than in English. Keil renders it, should thy word then come to pass, what will be the manner of the boy, and his doing? Ellicott gives the literal sense — what shall be the ordering of the child, and his work — the noun elsewhere meaning a right or a due, here the treatment belonging to a boy. Gill reads the opening clause, now let thy words come to pass, as not a wish merely but a prayer of faith. The answer does not answer. Gill observes that the angel returns no direct word either about what should be done to the child or what the child should do, but only repeats what he had said to the woman, which she would observe and which was enough for him to know. Keil marks the single addition made this second time, the caution against eating anything that comes of the vine, bringing the charge into line with the law of the Nazarite in Numbers — where the separation is spelled out to the last particular, no vinegar of wine, no grapes moist or dried, nothing of the vine from the kernels to the husk. Ellicott sums up the visit shortly and probably rightly: the object seems only to have been to give Manoah certainty.
15:
Gill has Manoah speak just as he sees the visitor means to say no more and is about to leave. What he offers is a kid, and the commentators cannot agree what he intended by it. Clarke reads it simply: not knowing the man's quality, Manoah meant hospitality. Ellicott finds the language genuinely ambiguous. The phrase is literally before thy face, the narrative runs parallel to the angel's appearance to Gideon, and the same uncertainty attaches to the terms, since the Hebrew verb, like the Greek and Latin answering to it, may mean either to do or to sacrifice; so we cannot decide whether a sacrifice or a meal was meant. He adds that a kid was a special delicacy. Henry takes the offer as gratitude and draws a rule — those who welcome the message will be kind to the messengers for the sake of him who sends them. The angel declines, as he had declined Gideon's, and turns the meal into an offering. Angels need neither meat nor drink, Henry observes; the glorifying of God is their meat and drink, as it was Christ's own. And we do God's will in some measure as they do if, though we cannot live without eating, we eat and drink to his glory, and so turn our common meals into sacrifices.

That Manoah did not know whom he spoke to Henry counts a mercy, not an oversight. It was in kindness that the angel's nature was concealed while he stood there, for had Manoah known it the terror would have been such that he durst not have conversed with him. So Christ was in the world and the world knew him not; verily thou art a God that hidest thyself. We could not bear the sight of the divine glory unveiled; and God, having determined to speak to us by men like ourselves, took care that even when he spoke by his angels or by his Son they should appear in the likeness of men, and be taken for no more than men of God.

The refusal of the name Henry treats as the most instructive thing in the chapter. Manoah's motive was not doubt: he wanted the man's name and tribe so they might return the visit, and that when the sayings came to pass they might do him honour — celebrate him as a true prophet, name the child after him, or send a present. It is a good desire, honestly meant, and it is refused. Why askest thou thus after my name? Jacob could not prevail for that favour either. We have not what we ask, Henry says, when we ask we know not what; and he draws the distinction that governs the episode. What Manoah asked for the direction of his duty he was readily told; what he asked to gratify curiosity was refused. God has given full direction concerning our duty in his word, but never designed to answer all the enquiries of a speculative head. The reason given is that the name is secret — and Henry explains historically that the names of angels were not yet revealed, to prevent men idolizing them. After the captivity, when the church was cured of idolatry, angels made themselves known to Daniel by name, and to Zacharias one gave his name unasked, I am Gabriel. But the word rendered secret may equally be rendered wonderful, and Henry takes that sense too, since one of Christ's names is Wonderful — a name long secret, brought to light by the gospel. Manoah must not ask because he must not know: there are secret things which do not belong to us, and about which we must be content to remain in the dark; nor should we indulge a vain curiosity concerning them, since to be willingly ignorant of what our great Master refuses to teach is a learned kind of ignorance.
16:
Clarke reads the angel's refusal as two in one: as a spiritual being he does not subsist by earthly food, and neither will he receive the homage belonging to God, so the burnt offering must go to Jehovah. Ellicott makes the second half the more pointed: angels invariably discourage and reprove the worship of angels that the early Gnostic sects tended toward. But he will not have the first pressed too far, since the angel might have partaken of earthly food, as the visitors to Abraham and Lot did; and he quotes Milton, that these pure intelligential substances require food as your rational does. Keil parses the next question closely. It reads literally who is thy name, the pronoun asking after a person rather than a nature; and the verb rendered do thee honour means to honour by presents. Ellicott says the same more briefly — especially by a gift, the commonest Eastern sense of the word.

The answer turns on a single Hebrew adjective, which all three handle. Keil sets out the written and read forms and concludes the word is not the angel's proper name but expresses the character of his name; and since a name denotes the nature, it expresses the peculiarity of his nature too. He insists it be taken absolutely — supremely wonderful, a predicate belonging to God alone, as in the great name of Isaiah — and refuses Bertheau's toning it down to mean something neither easy to utter nor easy to comprehend. Clarke turns the point the other way and makes it evidential. It was precisely because the name was secret that they wished to know it; but the angel does not say it is secret, he says it is Wonderful, the very character given to Jesus Christ by the prophet — and some suppose he gives this as his name, and so was our blessed Lord. Ellicott holds the middle ground: the word is an adjective, not the actual name — and he adds the observation that settles it for him, that the only angel who names himself anywhere in Scripture is Gabriel.

What follows is the miracle. Gill has Manoah fetch the kid he meant for a meal and bring it as a burnt offering, joining a meat offering as was usual. Keil explains why the rock is called an altar in the next verse: the angel of the Lord, being of one nature with God, sanctified it as an altar by the miraculous acceptance of the sacrifice — and the wonder is spelled out in what follows, the flame going up toward heaven and the angel ascending in it. Ellicott marks the change of word exactly: the rock of one verse is hallowed into an altar in the next. Clarke ties the miracle to the name: he acted according to what he was called, and being wonderful did wonderful things, probably causing fire to rise from the rock to consume the sacrifice and then ascending in the flame. Then comes the exchange that closes the chapter. Manoah concludes they must die, having seen God; and Gill observes his wife was the less fearful and the stronger believer, comforting him with three arguments — that if the Lord had meant to kill them he would not have received their offering, nor shown them all these things, nor told them such things at such a time. Clarke calls this excellent reasoning and turns it into counsel for dark dispensations of providence: he who has preserved and borne with a man so long is not less willing to save him now, and he who gave his Son to redeem him can never be indifferent to his welfare — indeed the very light that shows a man his wretchedness proves God waiting to be gracious, and the penitential pangs he feels argue the fire is of God's kindling, sent to refine and not destroy.
24:
The child's name sets off the widest disagreement here. Josephus rendered it strong, and Ellicott suspects he was not unwilling to hint an analogy with the Greek Hercules; Keil follows the same line, rejecting sun-like or hero of the sun and deriving the word from a root meaning to be strong or daring. Jerome made it strength of the sun, compounding sun and strength. Gill will not allow the word carries strength in it and takes it from the sun, offering three reasons why it might have been given — the splendour of the child's countenance at birth, the memory of the angel's shining countenance, or the darkness of the calamity he was to dispel. Clarke traces it to a root meaning to serve, making it either a little sun or a little servant, and prefers the second as just the name maternal fondness would impose on an only son. Ellicott thinks sunny the likeliest sense, and notes the rabbis said the boy was named after the name of God, who is called a sun and shield to Israel. He marks too a point easily passed over: here the mother gave the name.

Henry takes the name as a type. He derives it from the word for sun turned into a diminutive — a little sun — and finds several reasons: that Samson, like Moses, was born to deliver and was exceedingly fair, his face shining like a small sun; that his parents may have named him in memory of the man of God's shining countenance; and that if the sun may be compared to a strong man running his race, a strong man may as fairly be compared to the sun. He ends on Samson as the glory of and a light to his people, a type of Christ the Sun of righteousness. On the growth that follows, Henry says the boy outgrew others of his age in strength and stature and more besides, so it appeared the Lord blessed him and was fitting him in body and mind for something extraordinary — children of promise shall have the blessing. Ellicott cautions against making too much of it. God has many kinds of blessing, and those alluded to here appear to be health, strength and courage; they by no means set Samson on a level with Samuel or John the Baptist.

The last verse turns on a verb of violence. Keil renders it that the Spirit of Jehovah began to thrust him, taking possession of him suddenly and impelling him to put forth supernatural powers; Ellicott glosses it as to agitate or thrust, following Luther, and adds that it implies vehement impulses to noble deeds — which came on him only at times. The Targum of Jonathan paraphrases it, Ellicott thinks rightly, as the spirit of courage from Jehovah; and he cites Amos ranking Nazarites with prophets, since however their modes differ they agree in a belief that strings every power to its highest tension, that they are Jehovah's own by a special calling. Clarke supplies the human side: Samson felt the degrading bondage of his countrymen and a desire to do something for their deliverance, and these feelings he had from the divine Spirit. Where the camp of Dan lay neither Keil nor Ellicott can say, Mahaneh-dan and Eshtaol being unidentified. Henry makes the closing observation, the best in the chapter. The Spirit moved him at times, not at all times, but as the wind blows where it lists — which shows what he did was not from himself, for then he could have done it whenever he pleased. Strong men think themselves greatly animated by wine, Henry adds; but Samson drank none and yet excelled in strength and courage, because the Spirit of God moved him. Therefore be not drunk with wine, but filled with the Spirit, who comes to the sober and temperate.
